The proposed project is a Voluntary Project Activity (VPA) focused on afforestation and will be implemented in Odisha, India. It aims to sequester atmospheric carbon dioxide through plantations. The project will promote native and climate-resilient species, with the special emphasis to support sustainable livelihoods through community participation and agroforestry practices. It will also enhance biodiversity and improve soil health. Furthermore, the project generates temporary employment for local communities during the implementation and management of the plantation. The project aligns with multiple SDGs, including climate action, life on land, and no poverty.

Project Saladillo transforms 15,946 hectares of cattle grazing land, subject to continual slash-and-burn practices, in Paraguay’s Cordillera region into a mosaic plantation combining commercial and conservation forestry. It prioritises long-term ecological resilience and sustainable development. The project integrates 25% permanent conservation with 75% selectively harvested forestry, maintaining at least 96% continuous forest cover. This model prevents deforestation by producing sustainable timber and biomass, while enhancing biodiversity through protection of native forests and riparian corridors, supporting habitat continuity and safeguarding local fauna. An estimated 1,122,437 tons of CO₂ will be sequestered over 50+ years. High-precision carbon monitoring uses LiDAR-based models calibrated with field sampling to ensure accuracy in both accessible and remote areas. Saladillo generates formal, year-round employment through staggered planting and harvesting, eliminating informal labour, reducing seasonal risks, and ensuring steady income for local communities. It collaborates closely with local NGOs such as Fundación Moisés Bertoni and the University of Asunción, integrating community engagement, biodiversity monitoring, and academic research. The project adheres to the highest environmental and social safeguards, aligning with FSC certification, IFC Performance Standards, and World Bank guidelines, contributing to SDGs 8, 12, 13, and 15.

The project aims to promote agroforestry practices by planting coconut trees (Cocos nucifera) on fallow farmland systems in the Indian state of Karnataka. The project developer Sow & Reap Agro Pvt. Ltd. aims to achieve the goals of (a) enhancing farmer income through climate resilient systems, and (b) mitigate the impact of climate change by sequestering atmospheric CO2 into coconut tree biomass.

The Madad Electric Cookstove (MEC) Project is abased clean energy initiative developed by Third Pole Solutions in partnership with the Aga Khan Rural Support Programme (AKRSP) as the coordinating and implementing agency in Pakistan. The project aims to replace traditional wood-burning stoves—locally known as bukhari—and 3-stone cooking methods with energy-efficient electric cookstoves. The Primary objectives of the Project is to reduce the use of wood for cooking, thereby reducing the GHG emissions and having a positive impact on the Climate (SDG 13). By adopting clean, sustainable cooking practices (SDG7), the Project will focus on ensuring healthy lives and promoting well-being for all by addressing the impact of environment factors on health (SDG3), reduce time spent on collecting or buying firewood resulting in cost savings and increasing the household's disposable income (SDG1) and promote gender equality by involving women's community groups (SDG5)

The proposed initiative is a Voluntary Project Activity (VPA) focused on agroforestry plantations, to be implemented in Odisha, India. This PoA aims to save water and reduce methane emissions during rice farming by introducing water management technology to rice farming, which is one of the main greenhouse gas emission sources in Cambodia. By participating in this project, farmers can produce low-carbon rice without reducing rice productivity and participate in mitigating climate change. ThanksCarbon, a business developer, has introduced an AI-based satellite technology into this project to reduce the burden on individual farmers for data collection and improve the convenience of monitoring data collection and MRV transparency. Farmers will be motivated and trained to refrain from continuously flooding their fields by putting the suggested AWD technology into effect, which would cut down on the quantity of CH4 emissions that would have been produced in the baseline situation. The sole change made to the project scenario is the adoption of alternating wetting and drying conditions rather than the submerged condition. Other than that, the project keeps the current agricultural techniques in place and does not introduce any new activities that might increase greenhouse gas emissions.

This is a Programme of Activities (PoA) called “GS PoA for Sustainable Rice Cultivation Projects in India” in India that will include various Voluntary Project Activities (VPAs) in it. The “GS PoA for Sustainable Rice Cultivation Projects in India” consists of implementation of Alternate and Wetting and Drying (AWD) practice in India. Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) method and aerobic rice cultivation method is a scientifically proven way of managing rice fields for better water management and achieving reduction or avoidance of methane emissions that is caused in traditional submerged rice fields. Therefore, Landmark Agri Exports Pvt. Ltd. (an Indian entity) & WeAct Pty Ltd. (an Australian entity) has taken a voluntary initiative to develop a project in India that is designed specifically for Rice fields to adopt AWD and other adjusted water managements methods, to be implemented across various states of India. Thus, the main objective of the project is to avoid flooded irrigation in rice fields and adopt AWD/other adjusted water management methods for rice cultivation to reduce methane emissions from the rice fields.

The proposed project activity is the voluntary action undertaken by Landmark Agri Exports Pvt. Ltd., and WeAct Pty Ltd. The project falls under the Agriculture category introducing improved agricultural practices in rice cultivation. This project aims to reduce methane (CH4) emissions through improved water management practices involving alternate wetting and drying (AWD) of the paddy lands. AWD is a proven method to reduce CH4 emission by as much as 48% compared to continuously flooded conditions where high rates of CH4 are emitted by the lands due to the anaerobic decomposition of the organic matter . Rice is the most prominent food crop in India. It is the backbone of livelihood for millions of rural households and plays a vital role in the country’s food security. India is one of the world's largest producers and exporters of rice and hence plays an important part in the country’s economy. The proposed VPA activity is planned to be implemented in the Madhya Pradesh State of India. This VPA is implemented in Seoni district covering 26,103 ha in 8 tahsils

Overall, the PoA will contribute to reduced greenhouse gas emissions, promote sustainable farming practices, and support environmental and economic sustainability.

In addition to promoting AWD, the VPA will support participating farmers with a comprehensive package of best practices tailored to optimize rice cultivation in the region.

The Programme of Activities (PoA), titled 'Sustainable Rice Production in South East and South Asia', is a multi-country initiative that promotes the adoption of a suite of sustainable agricultural practices. The project's core measure is Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD), a climate-smart irrigation technique aimed at reducing methane emissions and conserving water in rice fields. While initial implementation is focused on rice-growing regions in Indonesia and Vietnam, the project is designed with a long-term vision to scale across other countries in South and Southeast Asia. The primary goal is to generate quantifiable carbon and water benefits, with a broader aim to improve the overall environmental and social sustainability of rice farming by incorporating measures that address soil health, energy efficiency, and pollution control.

The VPA for Indonesia, a foundational component of the overarching PoA, focuses on promoting sustainable rice production. The project seeks to promote agroforestry in rural areas of India. The project's focus is to improve livelihood of the farmer community by enhancing their social and economic status. The project avoids environmental degradation by reducing synthetic fertilizer dependency and preventing land degradation.

The FS BECCS project, proposed under the Gold Standard for Global Goals (GS4GG), reflects FS – Fueling Sustainability’s ambition to lead Brazil’s energy transition with innovation, technical excellence, and private investment. Founded in 2017, FS is the third-largest ethanol producer in the country, operating modern plants in Mato Grosso. At its Lucas do Rio Verde facility, FS will capture biogenic CO₂ from corn ethanol fermentation. The stream, with about 98% purity, will be compressed, dehydrated, and injected into deep geological formations of the Parecis Basin for secure, long-term storage. As this CO₂ originates from the atmosphere via photosynthesis, its storage delivers net carbon removals. Project development followed four phases: Phase 1 (2019–2020) confirmed storage potential through feasibility studies and 2D seismic data. Phase 2 (2020–2022) added a 3D seismic survey and design of capture and compression systems. Phase 3 (2022–2024) drilled a stratigraphic well, collected geological data, and began equipment procurement. Phase 4 (2024–2026), now underway, includes injectivity tests, well conversion, monitoring infrastructure, and capture system construction. Commercial operations are expected in 2025, with carbon injection June 2026.

The sustainable rice cultivation VPA utilizing Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) technology has been initiated in Gazipur district, Bangladesh. This method effectively reduces methane emissions by introducing periodic soil aeration, disrupting the anaerobic conditions that typically lead to methane production. By enhancing soil conditions and promoting efficient water use, AWD contributes to greater resilience against climate variability, positioning it as a sustainable and climate-smart solution for rice farming.

The VPA promotes the use of Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) technology, which delivers both environmental and socio-economic benefits across Naogaon district of Bangladesh. Overall, AWD supports more efficient water management, lower greenhouse gas emissions, encourage sustainable agricultural practices, and contribute to long-term environmental and economic resilience.

The Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) VPA is designed to encourage eco-friendly rice farming methods in Natore district of Bangladesh, with a focus on cutting greenhouse gas emissions and enhancing water use efficiency. The VPA on sustainable rice cultivation using Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) technology is implemented in Netrokona district of Bangladesh. The process significantly reduces methane emissions by introducing aeration periods in the soil, breaking the anaerobic conditions that promote methane generation. As a result, AWD supports higher resilience to climate variability, making it an ideal sustainable solution for rice cultivation.

The VPA aims to reduce methane emissions from rice cultivation through the implementation of the Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) technique. This small-scale Gold Standard VPA is located in the Narsingdi district of Bangladesh. The objective of the initiative is to introduce AWD, a water-saving irrigation method on rice fields managed by smallholder farmers who currently practice continuous flooding (CF) thereby supporting climate resilient agricultural practices.

The Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) VPA is designed to encourage eco-friendly rice farming methods in Mymensingh district of Bangladesh, with a focus on cutting greenhouse gas emissions and enhancing water use efficiency. This project introduces Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) as a climate-smart water management practice in rice farming in Dong Thap Province, a major rice-producing area of the Mekong Delta. The project aims to reduce methane emissions from rice cultivation, save irrigation water, and support sustainable rice production. It is being implemented by Rikolto in Vietnam acting on behalf of Livelihoods Carbon Fund (LCF3). The core technical intervention of the project is the application of AWD, a water-saving irrigation technique that reduces methane emissions in rice cultivation. Instead of keeping rice paddies continuously flooded, AWD involves allowing the field to dry intermittently, typically until the water level drops 15 cm below the soil surface, at which point irrigation is resumed with a shallow flood of 2–5 cm. This practice reduces the anaerobic conditions in the soil that are responsible for methane generation, without negatively affecting rice yields. To support this method, the project installs PVC monitoring tubes (commonly known as pani-pipes) in farmers’ fields. These tools allow farmers to visually monitor the water level in the soil and make informed irrigation decisions, making AWD both accessible and easy to implement. In addition to water management, the project promotes improved straw and fertilizer practices. Rather than incorporating straw into the soil, which significantly contributes to methane emissions, farmers are encouraged to remove, compost, or repurpose straw for other uses such as mushroom cultivation. Fertilizer use is also optimized to improve nitrogen efficiency and reduce emissions of nitrous oxide (N₂O), another potent greenhouse gas.

The Khonobod 1-2 Utility-Scale Solar Photovoltaic (PV) Project is a large-scale renewable energy initiative designed to support Uzbekistan's transition toward clean energy and contribute to the global effort to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. The purpose of the project is to generate electricity by using clean solar power resources to meet the national electricity demand. The project will contribute to the reduction of GHG emission by displacing part with fossil fuel fired power plants of the generated electricity by the Grid. The expected annual GHG emission reductions over the first crediting period are 554,070 tCO2e/yr, which will contribute to the alleviation of climate change effects. The Khonobod 1-2 Solar PV Project will contribute to the achievement of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), SDG 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy), SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth) and SDG 13 (Climate Action).

The bundled project implemented by AES comprises two renewable power plants: Cristales, which generates electricity exclusively from solar energy, and Pampas, which utilizes both wind and solar resources. Both projects will be located in northern Chile, specifically in the Antofagasta Region, within the Atacama Desert. The project activities include the construction and operation of the generation plants, each equipped with Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS). The installed capacities for Pampas are 120 MW for wind, 230 MW for PV, and 340 MW for BESS, while for Cristales (previously referred to as Andes III) they are 287 MW for PV and 340 MW for BESS.

Sistema.bio is a social enterprise that provides access to innovative biodigester technology, training and financing to address the challenges of poverty, food security, and climate change. Sistema.bio manufactures and distributes high-quality, affordable biodigesters that enable farmers around the world to convert waste into energy and fertilizer, and works with farmers to ensure they become more sustainable, independent, and productive while mitigating the carbon emissions generated by agricultural activities. This project will provide a wide range of social, economic and environmental benefits for families and communities in India through the installation of biodigesters. The project includes various sizes of biodigesters to adjust to the different types of farmers. The project will focus on smallholder dairy farmers in the country, especially subsistence farmers who typically use woodfuel or LPG for their energy needs both in the household and productive uses in the farm, and who currently do not manage the manure generated by their animals and have either solid or liquid storage practices for this.

The Program of Activities, "Cova Safe Water Program in Central America" will provide safe water to rural communities in Central America with the first carbon project beginning in Honduras. Cova installs zero-emission water treatment technologies (in-line chlorination) to existing water supply systems. The resulting safe water replaces the need to burn non-renewable biomass in water boiling for purification of the water. This avoidance of fuel combustion reduces Greenhouse Gas (GHG) emissions and contributes to climate change goals.

The VPA, "Cova Safe Water Project - Honduras," provides safe water to rural communities in Honduras. Cova installs zero-emission water treatment technologies (in-line chlorination) to existing water supply systems. The resulting safe water replaces the need to burn non-renewable biomass by end-users in water boiling for purification of water. This avoidance of fuel combustion reduces Greenhouse Gas (GHG) emissions and contributes to climate change goals.

Under this project activity, VISION GREENEN Tech Pvt Ltd is developing an improved cookstoves program “Sustainable Cooking Solutions for Rural Communities: Madhya Pradesh Initiative” and aims to distribute improved cookstoves (ICS) to rural households in the Dhar and Khargone districts of Madhya Pradesh. The target beneficiaries of the program will be low-income & firewood-using households residing in villages of Dhar and Khargone districts of Madhya Pradesh. The Project intends to reach households that are currently using inefficient traditional cookstoves for cooking their meals. Households will be provided with improved cookstoves. ICS improves the combustion efficiency and thermal transfer to the cooking pot compared with a traditional stove, thereby reducing fuel usage. As a result, this project will contribute to SDGs including SDG 3 (Good Health and Well Being), SDG 4 (Quality Education), SDG 5 (Gender Equality), SDG 7 (Affordable and Clean energy), SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth), SDG 13 (Climate Action) and SDG 15 (Life on Land), in both quantitative and qualitative ways.

The purpose of the Voluntary Project Activity (VPA) is to provide safe drinking water to households in rural communities of Cambodia. This initiative intends to diminish the reliance on non-renewable biomass for water purification, which would otherwise be necessary in the absence of this project. The project aims to achieve this by deploying automated chlorination units, UV disinfection, and utilizing advanced IoT and AI-ML driven cloud technology for real-time water quality monitoring.

The Electric Cooking Program in Bangladesh by ATEC aims to replace highly polluting non-renewable and fossil cooking fuels with clean, efficient electric cooking solutions. The project will distribute and install ATEC’s patented eCook—an electric cookstove equipped with GSM connectivity that enables 100% digital MRV through ATEC’s dashboard. The primary beneficiaries are households that currently cook with biomass but are already connected to the national grid. By transitioning to efficient electric cooking, the project will offer households an affordable, convenient, and safe cooking alternative while contributing to SDGs 1, 3, 5, 7, 8, and 13. Project Description: Distribution and installation of eCook units with GSM and 100% dMRV capabilities. ATEC will lead project development and implementation and local implementation partners will support VPA management in Bangladesh. The project is voluntary and will apply the Methodology for Metered & Measured Energy Cooking Devices v1.2 for calculating emission reductions. The project will replace unsustainable biomass-based cooking—often practiced on inefficient three-stone fires and traditional stoves—with efficient electric cookstoves, thereby reducing GHG emissions and negative environmental and health impacts.

The goal of the “Community Program for the Preservation and Restoration of Mangroves” is to implement projects for the restoration of degraded mangrove and coastal/freshwater wetlands ecosystems. The aim is to recover ecological functionality by re-establishing hydrological connectivity, improving biodiversity, and removing atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂) through natural carbon sequestration processes. VPAs included under the PoA will be selected where degradation is demonstrated and restoration is technically feasible, prioritizing actions such as hydrological reconnection, assisted natural regeneration, and targeted enrichment planting with native species, together with the maintenance and monitoring required for durable outcomes. The aim is to restore ecological processes (water exchange, sediment dynamics, recruitment), enhance biodiversity, and remove CO₂ through conservative, verified sequestration in line with Gold Standard requirements.

The "Mangrove Restoration Project of 500 Hectares" is the first of several expected voluntary project activities (VPAs) to be included under the broader framework of the Programme of Activities (PoA) “Community Program for the Preservation and Restoration of Mangroves”. The project consists of the ecological restoration of 500.87 hectares of degraded mangrove ecosystems. The total project area consists of 500.87 ha, out of which 431.14 ha are eligible (degraded and transitional mangrove). Restoration measures include the reconnection of blocked tidal channels and removal of sediment plugs, assisted natural regeneration where hydrological conditions permit, and enrichment planting with native species.

Chishang, nestled in Taitung County, Taiwan, is renowned as a premier rice production region with a legacy of more than 70 years. The area’s lush paddies and traditional agricultural rhythms are stewarded by the Wanan Community Development Association (WACDA), an active local group established three decades ago. WACDA’s mission centers on environmental protection, cultural conservation, and the promotion of organic farming—principles that have guided community action and land management for generations. Typical farming practices in Chishang after the second rice harvest in late October include thorough removal of litter and several rounds of tillage, followed by maintaining clear, fallow fields until February. This period of rest for the land helps sanitize soil-borne disease bacteria. However, to manage weeds during this time, herbicides have traditionally been applied, reflecting both pragmatic and conventional approaches to field management. In recent years, Chishang’s farmers, under WACDA’s leadership, have begun to embrace more sustainable soil management techniques. Inspired by the Gold Standard for Global Goals (GS4GG) Soil Organic Carbon Framework Methodology, the community has adopted Cover Crops and Improved Tillage Activity Modules. These practices promise enhanced outcomes for both food security and climate resilience, by increasing soil carbon, reducing chemical use, and supporting ecosystem health.

Overview The US SecondCropTM Microbial Carbon Removal project represents a pioneering approach in agriculture-based carbon removal and is centered around the use of proprietary microbial technology to improve soil health and drive long-term carbon sequestration. The project transforms conventional farmland into durable carbon sinks by enhancing stable soil carbon, producing measurable climate and soil health outcomes. A key innovation in this program is the deployment of CarbonBuilderTM, a proprietary microbial inoculant developed by Loam Bio (refer to Appendix 5 - CarbonBuilder Development Stages at Loam Bio for a detailed summary of the product development pipeline). CarbonBuilder is applied as a seed treatment to enhance plant fertility, promote soil health, and increase the sequestration of soil organic carbon by reintroducing beneficial fungi into the soil. The US SecondCrop Microbial Carbon Removal project represents a grouped project comprising 36 farms. Participating farms are located in Illinois, Iowa, Minnesota, Nebraska, South Dakota and Wisconsin with a median farm size of 550 acres. All farms in the project are historically and currently used for cropping, primarily under a corn-soy rotation. Prior to the implementation of this project, there were no equivalent initiatives in the region focused on stable soil organic carbon sequestration. Agricultural practices in the U.S. Midwest were predominantly conventional, characterized by routine tillage and heavy reliance on synthetic fertilizers. The baseline scenario assumes the continuation of these practices in the absence of the project, leading to higher emissions and declining soil resilience over time. Under the project, participating farmers apply CarbonBuilder to applicable crops each year at the time of planting. Unlike conventional soil carbon projects that depend only on practice changes (no-till, cover crops), Loam’s inoculant accelerates microbial-fungal-root interactions that channel plant carbon into mineral- associated organic matter (MAOM) and aggregate-associated organic matter. Building stronger soil health in agricultural landscapes within United States Regenerative agricultural practices hold immense potential for higher adoption rates among farmers in the U.S. Midwest, a region characterized by its flat topography and fertile mollisol soils that are ideal for large-scale, mechanized farming (USDA NRCS). Historically, conventional farming in this area has relied on intensive tillage and heavy use of synthetic fertilizers to maximize yields. However, this has led to higher emissions and declining soil resilience over time. A study in the journal Earth's Future found that agricultural fields in the Midwestern U.S. have lost an average of two millimeters of soil per year since Euro-American settlement, nearly double the rate the USDA considers sustainable. It has been estimated that over the last 160 years, the region has lost approximately 57.6 trillion metric tons of topsoil, with plowing activities cited as the major culprit (Thaler et al. 2022). Similarly, research published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) revealed that the Midwest Corn Belt has lost its topsoil (A-horizon soil) from roughly one-third of its cultivated area, a significantly higher estimate than previous soil surveys indicated. This soil loss has removed 1.4 ± 0.5 petagrams of carbon from hillslopes, reducing crop yields in the study area by around 6% and causing billions in annual economic losses (Thaler et al. 2021). Poor soil health has a significant impact on productivity and the broader agricultural economy. The shift to regenerative practices including reduced or no-tillage, cover cropping, and the use of bio-stimulants, is therefore crucial for improving soil health, enhancing water retention, and mitigating climate change through potential widespread carbon removal and long-term sequestration. The project will install efficient Improved Cook Stoves (ICS) in firewood-dependent households in designated Nepal areas, replacing traditional cookstoves to reduce indoor air pollution and GHG emissions. The PoA will be implemented in Nepal.

The project will install efficient Improved Cook Stoves (ICS) in firewood-dependent households in designated Nepal areas, replacing traditional cookstoves to reduce indoor air pollution and GHG emissions. The VPA will be implemented within several municipalities in Lumbini Province of Nepal.

The proposed project activity aims to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions at the Lam Thach Cement Plant through the introduction of alternative fuels and clinker optimization measures. The project will replace a portion of fossil fuels traditionally used in the cement kiln with waste-derived fuels such as refuse-derived fuel (RDF) and dewatered sludge, which would otherwise be landfilled or improperly disposed. This substitution reduces CO₂ emissions associated with fossil fuel combustion and supports improved waste management practices. In addition, the project will lower process emissions by decreasing the clinker-to-cement ratio through the increased use of suitable supplementary cementitious materials. This results in reduced calcination-related CO₂ emissions from clinker production. The combined interventions contribute to a significant reduction in the carbon intensity of cement manufacturing at Lam Thach. The initiative supports Vietnam’s climate and circular economy objectives by diverting waste from landfills, reducing fossil fuel dependence, and promoting more efficient resource use. The overall project activity contributes to regional and national sustainable development.

Green Mining's PoA is based on operationalizing the collection, transportation, and destination of waste for recycling. In doing so, the PoA promotes the circular economy and prevents the environmental impacts of manufacturing new products from virgin material, ensuring greater energy efficiency in the production process and, thus, reducing associated Greenhouse Gas (GHG) emissions. The PoA is located in Brazil, and its operations are organized around receiving centers strategically placed in areas with high post-consumer waste generation. These centers receive, weigh, and properly store waste brought by registered local waste pickers, providing them fair compensation in a way that prioritizes the social inclusion of people in vulnerable situations. In this regard, the PoA stands out for its disruptive nature, passing on the full value of waste to registered waste pickers and expanding the positive social impact of recycling. Once properly registered, the waste is transported to the plants responsible for the recycling process, ensuring its subsequent reinsertion into the production chain. This PoA constitutes, therefore, an overarching framework aimed at promoting recycling in Brazil in an inclusive and sustainable manner.

The CDR ORINOQUÍA project, developed by Biofix Consultoría S.A.S BIC, is a large-scale afforestation, reforestation, and revegetation (ARR) initiative designed to mitigate climate change by restoring degraded savannah ecosystems in the Orinoco region of Colombia. The project covers 8,441 hectares across seven private properties (Arizona, La Fortuna, La Carolina, San Andrés, Villa Claudia, Buenos Aires, and San Miguel) located in Puerto Gaitán, Meta. The project employs a dual reforestation strategy: Forest Plantations: Establishment of non-native species (Eucalyptus pellita and Pinus caribaea). Natural Enrichment: Restoration of non-flood zones and flooded areas (gallery and moriche forests) using native species such as Cassia grandis, Hymenaea courbaril, Caraipa llanorum, Mauritia flexuosa, Euterpe precatoria, and Manilkara zapota. To achieve its goals, the project operates a permanent nursery producing over three million seedlings annually. Implementation includes specialized machinery for site preparation, alongside GPS and drone technology for precise monitoring. This integrated approach aims to increase carbon sequestration and generate certified carbon credits while contributing to SDG 13 (Climate Action), SDG 8 (Decent Work), SDG 5 (Gender Equality) and SDG 15 (Life on Land). The project boundary encompasses all land parcels dedicated to these ARR activities as GHG sinks.

Green Mining’s "GS23502 VPA-1 Factory Price Station" is a Real Case Voluntary Project Activity (VPA) that promotes the structured integration of informal waste collection into a formal recycling chain, with traceability, efficiency and environmental performance, while generating verifiable emission reductions. The VPA is physically located in Santo Amaro neighborhood, in the municipality of São Paulo, State of São Paulo, Brazil. The core project facilities consist of a waste logistics and aggregation unit where recyclable materials collected by local waste pickers are received, weighed, sorted, temporarily stored and transported to recycling plants, from which they are reintroduced into the production chain.

The purpose of the project is to install heat pumps in Kyrgyzstan. Heat pumps are modern devices used in heating, air conditioning and hot water applications. Unlike other heat generators (coal, gas, diesel and electric), the heat pump extracts (pumps out) low-potential energy from the environment (accumulated during the warm season from ground, groundwater, rocks etc) and increases the heat potential by transferring heat energy from a source with a lower temperature to a higher temperature via the thermodynamic steam-compression cycle. Heat pumps needs an external energy source, usually electricity, to operate. The most common design of a heat pump consists of a compressor, a thermal expansion valve, an evaporator and a condenser. The coolant circulating inside these components is called refrigerant. The project involves the installation of Heat pumps in its first phase in Bishkek and Chuy Region. These HPs replace energy-intensive heating solutions used in homes, and institutions which run on carbon-intensive and expensive fossil fuels.

The objective of the program is to support smallholder farmers and rural communities in adopting sustainable agroforestry practices, which involve planting trees alongside crops or on fallow land across India. These activities will help restore soil health, improve agricultural productivity, and generate long-term environmental and economic benefits. Farmers will retain full ownership and rights over the trees they plant and the outputs from those trees. Any profits from the planting of additional species (such as fruit or timber trees) will belong entirely to the farmers. In addition to the economic benefits, the project will also reduce vulnerability to climate change. By increasing tree cover, it will help combat land degradation, improve water retention, and enhance biodiversity. Furthermore, the program will provide farmers access to carbon credit revenue share, promoting sustainable land use while improving their long-term livelihoods

Reducing Methane Emissions through Improved Rice Cultivation in India Program of Activities (PoA), developed by Commonland B.V., aims to address one of the key sources of greenhouse gas emissions in agriculture: methane from rice farming. The POA aims to promote sustainable cultivation practices through promoting Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) and Direct Seeded Rice (DSR), as alternatives to conventional continuous flooding. By improving water management and soil conditions, the PoA seeks to reduce methane emissions, enhance climate resilience, and support farmer livelihoods across different regions of India.

The rice cultivation project in Kabirdham, India, is a joint effort between Commonland B.V. and Chhattisgarh Agricon Private Limited, aimed at promoting sustainable agricultural practices while reducing methane emissions. The initiative encourages farmers to adopt Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) and Direct Seeded Rice (DSR) techniques to replace conventional continuous flooding, which is a major source of methane emissions in rice farming. By improving water management and soil conditions, this project seeks to enhance agricultural sustainability and farmer livelihoods.

The Maldives Captive Solar Photovoltaic Renewable Energy Project involves the installation and operation of stand-alone rooftop solar photovoltaic (PV) systems at captive consumer facilities across the Maldives. The solar PV systems generate renewable electricity exclusively for on-site consumption. The project directly replaces electricity that would otherwise be produced using diesel-based generators, which are the primary source of power for captive and isolated facilities in the Maldives.
The Maldives Captive Solar Photovoltaic Renewable Energy Project involves the installation and operation of rooftop solar photovoltaic (PV) systems at captive consumer facilities across the Maldives.

The B4H Initiative is a sustainable energy project aimed at promoting renewable energy and waste management in rural households across two Indian states. The initiative involves the installation of 14,690 household biogas plants, primarily in Maharashtra (13,752 units) and Madhya Pradesh (938 units). These plants utilize animal dung to generate biogas for thermal energy, reducing greenhouse gas emissions and dependence on fossil fuels. The project adheres to the "Methodology for Animal Manure Management and Biogas Use for Thermal Energy Generation" (Version 1.1, released January 25, 2023). The Household biogas units are sized at 2m³ , 3m³ , and 4m³, enabling clean cooking and organic fertilizer production for beneficiaries. By addressing methane emissions from manure and providing affordable energy, B4H enhances livelihoods, improves air quality, and supports climate resilience in underserved communities. The initiative targets rural farmers, with installations verified through a detailed beneficiary database,to ensure long-term monitoring for carbon credit issuance.

The Proyecto Forestal Los Tualdos (Los Tualdos) is an environmental initiative aimed at transforming 204 hectares of degraded grassland by establishing sustainable forest plantations composed of both native and exotic species. By planting more than 152,000 trees and restoring local ecosystems, the project is expected to sequester approximately 105,000 tonnes of CO₂ equivalent over the next three decades.

The voluntary project activity (VPA) is a voluntary initiative by Unlocking Communities (UC) to distribute improved charcoal stoves in Haiti. The target beneficiaries under the project will be the households which were earlier dependent on charcoal based traditional stoves for cooking. Unlocking Communities is a locally run organization working in northern and central Haiti. Distribution of improved cookstove which is a clean energy product as compared to the baseline, will reduce the GHG emissions. The use of improved cookstove will offer several environmental and health benefits such as reduction in the levels of indoor air pollution (IAP), women drudgery, deforestation etc. thereby having a positive impact on the health of the community.

The Gold Standard “Nestlé & FNC Tree Planting Colombia” is a joint strategy between Nestlé and the National Federation of Coffee Growers of Colombia (FNC). It is implemented through the planting of trees on coffee farms that are part of Nestlé’s value chain and on neighboring farms located within the coffee-growing ecosystem. The project emerged as a mitigation and adaptation measure to prepare crops for the impacts of climate variability, contribute to the conservation of water and soils, enhance biodiversity, and serve as a nature-based solution for the removal of CO₂ from the atmosphere.

The voluntary project activity (VPA) is a voluntary initiative by Unlocking Communities (UC) to distribute institution water filters in Haiti. The use of water filters will offer several environmental and health benefits such as reduction in the levels of indoor air pollution (IAP), reduction in water borne diseases, deforestation etc. thereby having a positive impact on the health of the community.

The proposed GS project activity “CGR Guatapara Landfill Project” promotes destruction and utilization of landfill gas (LFG) (rich in methane) generated at the CGR Guatapará landfill, located in the municipality of Guatapará in São Paulo State (South-eastern region of Brazil). LFG destruction and utilization occurs through its collection and destruction in high temperature enclosed flare(s) and its utilization as gaseous fuel for electricity generation (in engine-generator sets installed at the CGR Guatapará landfill as part of the project activity) respectively. Thus, besides methane destruction, the project activity also promotes generation of electricity by using renewable energy source.

The proposed project activity aims to displace use of non-renewable fossil fuels such as fire wood, charcoal or LPG (Liquefied Petroleum Gas) for cooking with clean cooking technologies such as biogas unit (biodigester and biogas stove) in the households of various states of India.

The project activity titled “Proactiva CGA Iperó Landfill Gas to Energy Project” encompasses the promotion of destruction and utilization landfill gas (LFG) (rich in methane) at the CGA Iperó landfill site. LFG destruction occurs in a high temperature enclosed flare and through its utilization as gaseous fuel for electricity generation (in engine-generator sets). The CGA Iperó landfill is located located in the border of Sorocaba and Iperó’s municipalities, in São Paulo State, Southeastern Region of Brazil.

The Program Development Objective is to (i) reduce carbon emission and cost of operation for Thailand, (ii) improve air quality, and (iii) tap into the potential of the carbon market to offset the cost of investments with short-term and no regret interventions that are proposed to be implemented in the coming years to enable immediate actions of stakeholders to move towards a green and climate-resilient future. The program aims to support Thailand to reduce carbon emissions and move towards a green and climate resilient future through the following interventions: • Increasing renewable energy (RE) generation capacity for captive consumption • Improving energy efficiency (EE) in buildings • Upgrading to LED streetlights • Transition to electric vehicles

The proposed VPA aims to increase renewable energy generation capacity via solar photovoltaic (PV) installation in public and private buildings. Thailand has immense potential for solar-based projects. While large-scale solar farms require large land-use, rooftop solar can utilize the space on the rooftops of buildings or in and around as captive ground-mounted solar installations within the premises of the buildings in cities. Thus, installing solar for buildings is a practical measure to reduce emissions and energy demand for cities. The VPA entails the installation of rooftop and ground-mounted solar PV systems for captive (self-consumption) use in Thailand. The VPA will generate approximately 20,126 MWh annually and achieve 8,030 tCO2 in annual emission reductions.

KPC intends to develop a bamboo plantation designed to address socio-economic and environmental challenges in the Philippines. Bamboo is known for its high carbon sequestration capabilities. One of our goals is to contribute to greenhouse gas (GHG) removals thereby generating high integrity carbon credits representing verified greenhouse gas removals over the crediting period and also providing jobs and economic returns to the IP communities. The geographic region of the project is in Cotabato province in the Philippines within the two Municipalities of President Roxas and Arakan. The project will be implemented on IPs’ ancestral lands within the defined project boundary. The project will provide a sustainable and steady source of livelihood for IP communities that will help address rural poverty and will provide the new generation of IP’s better opportunities in life. It will foster rural development, strengthen food security, and promote social stability through sustainable employment generation. It will also foster collaboration between the private and public sectors to further develop the Philippine bamboo industry.

The US SecondCrop Project removes atmospheric CO₂ by applying CarbonBuilder, a patented fungal seed coating, to corn and soybean crops across US Midwest farmland. Root-associated fungi intercept plant-derived carbon and convert it into Mineral-Associated Organic Carbon (MAOC), physically bound to soil minerals and proven to persist for centuries. No land use change, new equipment, or altered crop rotations are required.

In Laos consistent access to safe, potable water remains a critical challenge, forcing many rural communities to rely on contaminated sources. To mitigate health risks, households traditionally boil water over biomass and charcoal fires—a practice that is labor intensive, environmentally taxing, and is a significant contributor to deforestation and indoor air pollution. TerraClear, a social enterprise based in Laos, addresses this issue through the manufacture and distribution of locally produced ceramic water filters. These gravity-fed household treatment systems require zero energy input, providing a sustainable, emissions-free alternative to traditional boiling. By replacing carbon-intensive water treatment with this clean technology, the project directly reduces greenhouse gas emissions and waterborne diseases while simultaneously improving school attendance and productivity. With the support of carbon finance, TerraClear will continue to scale its operations to reach hundreds of thousands of families and create sustainable jobs in rural areas, ensuring that clean water access no longer comes at the cost of vital forest resources.

The Granadillos Wind Park project consists of the development of a 50 MW wind power facility located in Villa Vázquez, Montecristi province, aimed at supplying renewable electricity to the national grid. The project is expected to generate approximately 153 GWh annually using wind turbines. It will contribute to climate change mitigation (SDG 13) and support access to affordable and clean energy (SDG 7). Additionally, it will promote economic growth and job creation (SDG 8), generating up to 350 jobs during construction and around 15 permanent positions during operation and maintenance.

The Matafongo Solar Park project consists of the development of a 50 MWac photovoltaic facility located in Sabana Buey village, Peravia province, aimed at supplying renewable electricity to the national grid (SENI). The project is expected to generate approximately 118 GWh annually and reduce around 80,000 tCO₂e per year. It will contribute to climate change mitigation (SDG 13) and support access to affordable and clean energy (SDG 7). Additionally, it will promote economic growth and job creation (SDG 8), generating up to 350 jobs during construction and around 15 permanent positions during operation and maintenance.

The purpose of this project is to modernize paddy cultivation in Bangladesh by promoting and implementing the alternate wetting and drying (AWD) method in project farms/areas. The AWD method promoted under the project is designed to optimize water usage in paddy cultivation by alternating periods of wetting and drying. This technique reduces water consumption and improves soil aeration, as a result methane emissions from paddy fields are significantly reduced contributing to lower greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions.

The “SCETA - Supporting a Sustainable Circular Economy Transition in Agriculture for Carbon Neutralization” aims to generate carbon credits through the enhancement of soil carbon sequestration in Kazakhstan. Improved sequestration is achieved by introducing sustainable agricultural practices to local farmers. The project provides advisory services and access to sustainable agricultural best practices, as well as implementation of an improved monitoring system to measure achieved results against the baseline.

The Belize Coastal Sargassum Resilience and Circularity Project aims to intercept and process sargassum biomass and eligible biodegradable organic matter to avoid methane emissions from uncontrolled decomposition and landfill disposal. The project combines controlled aerobic treatment, decentralized organic waste processing, and circular resource recovery to transform intercepted biomass into beneficial products, including biochar-enriched compost for local use. Implemented initially in Caye Caulker, Belize, in collaboration with local stakeholders, the project is designed to strengthen coastal resilience, support sustainable land management, reduce environmental impacts associated with sargassum accumulation, and contribute to measurable climate mitigation outcomes under Gold Standard methodologies.

The Amru Rice AWD Project in Cambodia supports the adoption of Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) in irrigated rice cultivation to reduce methane emissions while maintaining stable yields and farmer livelihoods. The project replaces continuous flooding with controlled wetting and drying cycles, using water-level pipes to guide irrigation timing and ensure safe drainage thresholds. By reducing anaerobic soil conditions in paddy fields, AWD can significantly lower methane emissions while also improving irrigation water efficiency. The project is expected to scale to beyond 20,000 hectares. The project is being co-developed by Amru Rice Cambodia and CarbonFarm, with both parties acting as project proponents. Amru Rice Cambodia leads on-ground implementation, while CarbonFarm supports as a technical partner through digital MRV tools, including satellite imagery, AI-based field monitoring, and selected IoT devices to strengthen data traceability.

In partnership with Hanns R. Neumann Stiftung, GrowGrounds is transforming coffee monocultures in Brazil’s Mantiqueira region into regenerative agroforestry systems that sequester carbon, restore biodiversity, and strengthen farm resilience. Over a 30-year period, the initiative will convert 500 to 1,500 hectares of coffee land and engage more than 200 smallholder farmers. By integrating trees into coffee systems compatible with mechanized harvesting and cattle grazing, the project provides a scalable model that improves soil health, enhances climate resilience, and supports landscape restoration. Beyond carbon sequestration, the project generates strong social and environmental benefits. Farmers receive 70% of carbon revenues, benefit from improved working conditions through shade-grown systems, and gain diversified long-term income opportunities. The project area borders the Serra do Papagaio State Park, a protected area of approx. 22,917 hectares within the Mantiqueira Mountain Range, a critical water source for southeastern Brazil. The park conserves remnants of the Atlantic Forest biome, one of the world’s most biodiverse and threatened ecosystems. To assess biodiversity impacts and guide monitoring, the project applies the IUCN's RHINO framework, with a focus on key species including the Maldonado Redbelly Toad, Buffy-tufted-ear marmoset, Ochre-breasted Pipit, Vinaceous-breasted Amazon, Sickle-winged Nightjar, and Luderwaldt's Highland Frog.

The project enables rice growing farmers in Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Telangana, Tamilnadu, West Bengal, Odisha and Chhattisgarh to transition from conventional continuously flooded rice cultivation to Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD). The core purpose is to reduce methane emissions from paddy fields while improving water efficiency, strengthening climate resilience, and increasing farmer livelihoods through a single scalable intervention. In the first instance the project is implemented in the Srikakulam and vizinagaram villages of Andhra Pradesh in 5,041 ha of land which reduces 6,710 tCO2e/year. Detail climate change mitigation/adaptation contributions Mitigation: The project delivers climate mitigation benefits by reducing methane generation in paddy fields. AWD shortens the duration of continuous flooding, allowing aerobic soil conditions to form, which: Significantly reduces methane emissions, the dominant emission source in irrigated paddy Lowers energy-related emissions due to reduced irrigation pumping demand Prevents soil carbon loss caused by over-flooding and anaerobic conditions The transition is expected to generate substantial emission reductions across all participating fields under the project boundary. Adaptation: AWD strengthens climate resilience in farming systems and communities by: Reducing water consumption, helping farmers cope with erratic rainfall and declining groundwater Improving soil aeration and root development, enabling crops to better tolerate climatic stress Lowering irrigation costs and farm expenses, increasing financial resilience Improving access to technical support and knowledge through farmer training and field demonstrations By promoting a climate-responsive irrigation practice, the project supports long-term adaptation to rising temperatures and water scarcity in Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Telangana, Tamilnadu, West Bengal, Odisha and Chhattisgarh of Indian states.

The project supports smallholder farmers in integrating agroforestry practices into existing agricultural lands to improve livelihoods, strengthen ecosystem resilience, and promote sustainable land management. The project involves planting and maintaining a mix of native fruit and timber tree species within farming systems. Fruit trees provide regular income and food security benefits, while timber species offer long-term economic value. These interventions also improve soil health, reduce soil erosion, enhance soil moisture retention, and increase vegetation cover. The project contributes to climate change mitigation through carbon sequestration in tree biomass and enhancement of soil organic carbon, generating measurable and verifiable greenhouse gas removals under the Gold Standard Land Use and Forests (LUF) framework. By diversifying farm income and restoring degraded landscapes, the project aims to deliver long-term climate, environmental, and socio-economic benefits for participating rural communities.

Net Zero Ag Limited plans a Programme of Activities that aims to reduce methane emissions associated with conventional farming (CF) techniques. The first small-scale project activities will start in Narowal and Mandi Bahauddin, Pakistan on May 2026. Rice cultivation is one of the main GHG sources within the agriculture sector and generates approximately 8.5 MtCO2e of methane per year — roughly 2% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Conventional flooding-based production practices generate significant methane emissions and consume large volumes of fresh water. The programme will introduce the technique of alternate wetting and drying (AWD) to rice farmers in Pakistan. By adaptation of the technique, controlled irrigation strategy implemented will significantly reduce methane emissions, water use, and pumping costs.

The primary objective of the Programme of Activities (PoA) is to establish and manage 10,000 ha of agroforestry plantations on croplands across the states of Gujarat and Rajasthan through the implementation of multiple Voluntary Project Activities (VPAs). The PoA aims to promote sustainable land-use practices by introduction of diverse tree species. Through active engagement with local farmers and stakeholders, the PoA initiative will not only sequester approximately 2,433,999 tonnes of CO2 equivalent over the crediting period but also plays a crucial role in developing resilient agroforestry systems that not only restore ecological balance but also deliver long-term social and economic benefits to local farmer communities. The first real case VPA under this PoA, implemented a small scale agroforestry plantation of 98 ha which sequesters 10,889 tonnes of CO2 equivalent over the crediting period across multiple districts of Gujarat, India, which involves the plantation of multiple agroforestry species on agricultural land. By actively engaging local farmers, the VPA seeks to create resilient agroforestry plantations that generate long term ecological, economic and social benefits for the community.

The project aims to provide households and institutions in Bhutan with electric cooking and space-heating technologies to reduce GHG emissions from the use of firewood, biomass, and fossil fuels. Developed under GS, the project will deliver verified emission reductions and socio-economic benefits. For cooking, the project targets low-income households, schools, monasteries, fodder preparation, and small commercial establishments, including rural and high-altitude communities. In the absence of the project, cooking needs are primarily met through firewood, traditional stoves, and LPG, resulting in emissions, pressure on forest resources, and indoor air pollution. The project promotes efficient electric cooking technologies, including induction and infrared cookstoves powered by grid electricity. This transition reduces fuel consumption and emissions while improving indoor air quality, reducing cooking time and costs, and enhancing health and well-being. For space heating, the programme promotes the replacement of traditional biomass-based heating systems with efficient electric heaters, particularly in colder regions where firewood is the primary heating fuel. The intervention reduces fuel use, emissions, and pressure on forests while improving thermal comfort, indoor air quality, and living conditions. It also reduces the time and costs associated with fuel collection and purchase, especially benefiting women and supporting Bhutan’s low-carbon development objectives.

The project will produce and distribute char-briquettes made from agricultural residues, primarily coconut shells, as a sustainable cooking fuel for households and street food vendors in Cambodia. Agricultural residues are crushed, carbonized in a rotary carbonization furnace, mixed with a binder, and pressed into uniform briquettes under high pressure. The project uses waste heat recovered from the pyrolysis process for drying, improving energy efficiency and ensuring low residual moisture and consistent product quality. The briquettes are intended to replace traditional wood charcoal, thereby reducing greenhouse gas emissions and pressure on forest resources.

The project proponent is Rossmann Beteiligungs GmbH. The project “Rossmann Nicaragua - Reforesting diverse native tree species in East Nicaragua” is an ambitious private-led environmental project aimed at transforming 936 hectares of degraded slash & burn land in the tropical lowland of East Nicaragua into a thriving, diverse native forest ecosystem. The project activities encompass an afforestation/reforestation activity that mitigates climate change: The establishment of a mainly native tree species reforestation at an area which has been used so far for cattle, applying „slash and burn“ practices for at least the last two decades. The cattle was grazing throughout the majority of the year and the bush was burned down and slashed frequently to enable new grass growth. The project does not only include the reforestation of 21 mainly native trees but also additional forest islands, 200 ha which were protected from slash & burn and are not eligible as project activities. They serve as biodiversity habitats and bridges for wandering animals seeking new habitats. The local communities in the neighborhoods will be involved in the project as additional jobs and benefits will be created. The project site will be operated by Ritter Sport Nicaragua, who represents an adjacent certified Gold Standard afforestation project.

Prithu is a climate-focused organization dedicated to advancing regenerative agriculture and nature-based carbon removal solutions. The company works with farmers, Farmer Producer Organizations (FPOs), Self-Help Groups (SHGs), and local institutions to implement sustainable land management practices that improve soil health while contributing to climate mitigation. Prithu’s approach combines scientific soil monitoring, community engagement, digital measurement systems, and internationally recognized carbon methodologies to ensure environmental integrity and transparent benefit sharing. The programme is being developed under the Gold Standard Programme of Activities (PoA) framework, allowing multiple project activities across India to be coordinated under a single programme while maintaining rigorous monitoring, reporting, and verification requirements. Launched as a long-term climate and agricultural sustainability initiative, the Prithu Soil Organic Carbon (SOC) Programme aims to support smallholder farmers in adopting regenerative agricultural practices, improving soil health, enhancing farm resilience, and generating additional income through high-quality carbon credits. The programme connects farmers to international carbon markets through scientifically robust, measurable, verifiable, and scalable soil carbon sequestration activities.

The Voluntary Project Activity (VPA) in Maharashtra aims to accelerate the adoption of regenerative agricultural practices that improve soil health, increase soil organic carbon sequestration, reduce greenhouse gas emissions, and strengthen the climate resilience of participating farming communities. Implemented under the Gold Standard Programme of Activities (PoA), the VPA will enable eligible farmers in Maharashtra to adopt sustainable land-management practices and access international voluntary carbon markets. Verified emission reductions and carbon removals generated through these practices will create an additional source of financial benefit for participating farmers. The Maharashtra VPA is the first activity proposed under the PoA. It will be implemented within the state in accordance with Gold Standard requirements, including the applicable methodology, eligibility criteria, monitoring, reporting and verification procedures. Additional VPAs may subsequently be developed under the same PoA in other Indian states and union territories, subject to the relevant Gold Standard requirements. Farmers voluntarily enrol in the programme and commit to adopting approved regenerative agricultural practices. Soil carbon levels are measured through periodic soil sampling and laboratory analysis, while project performance is monitored through a comprehensive Measurement, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) system.

Andes has developed a technology that captures atmospheric CO2 and converts it to inorganic carbon in the soil through the application of a microbial inoculant containing Bacillus sp. strain MP1 (Lascar). When applied to the soil, this inoculant enhances the natural carbon sequestration process, resulting in an increase in Soil Inorganic Carbon (SIC). The increase in SIC resulting from this microbial activity is carefully measured through direct soil samples over the season on both fields treated with the microbial inoculant and untreated baseline fields, adhering to the specified monitoring protocol of the Methodology. The Project’s impact is measured against a baseline scenario representing soil types and conditions without microbial inoculant application. Carbon removal is quantified by comparing Soil Inorganic Carbon (SIC) generation in treated versus baseline untreated units over the same growing season. Units are pooled and linked based on the key similarity criteria to determine carbon removed. The Project area spans across several agricultural sites within the USA Midwest. In 2026 the project targeted area exclusively in North Dakota, USA. Andes not only provides a practical solution to the pressing problem of greenhouse gas emissions but also offers local farmers an opportunity to actively contribute to global climate mitigation efforts and offers a host of co-benefits, including additional revenue stream for farmers and healthier soil and plants.

Solar Power Company Limited has constructed solar photovoltaic (PV) plants to supply clean renewable electricity to the Thailand grid. The goal of this small-scale CPA (SSC-CPA) is to facilitate the transition away from inefficient conventional biomass stoves by providing higher-efficiency and clean burning improved cooking biomass stoves (ICS) to households (“non-institutional") making residential use of the technology implemented. The baseline scenario was identified using data from a large scale national survey published by the United Nations Comisión Económica para América Latina y el Caribe (UN-CEPAL), report titled Consumo de Leña en Honduras (April 2011). This report shows that on average 69% of interviewed households used firewood as input for cooking food, and over 60% of baseline stove models are traditional designs that use woodfuel. This SSC-CPA aims to provide both climate and livelihood benefits to the large population of Honduran households currently using inefficient biomass burning stoves.Several greenhouse gases (GHG), including carbon dioxide, are produced as a result of the combustion of non-renewable biomass as used in cooking stoves. ICS improve heat transfer efficiency as compared to the baseline conventional stoves, thereby reducing both the amount of wood fuel used by unit appliance implemented and the emission of GHGs. In addition to direct climate benefits, this SSC-CPA achieves several co-benefits that contribute to sustainable development:Environmental BenefitsThe project reduces the demand for biomass required for cooking stoves thus reducing the rate of deforestation connected to wood consumption. In addition, the reduction in use of less efficient stoves will yield a reduction in emissions from fuel combustion thus improving air quality and reducing the emission of harmful gases that contribute to climate change.Social and economic benefitsProject beneficiaries using the ICS reduce their wood consumption. The reduction in fuel needs will also save project beneficiaries time and income. This means that biomass users who gather wood will see a reduction in the amount that they have to collect, leaving that time available for other activities. Biomass users that purchase their fuel will be able to direct more of their income to other needs. From the economic perspective, the project will contribute to the scale-up of local businesses and organizations, with the potential to create jobs in retail, marketing and distribution.

In Haiti more than 90% of the population cooks on charcoal-based stoves and do so using so called traditional ones. Such stoves are considered non-efficient and require large amount of charcoal to operate which translate into a significant cost for the user. More than 1.4 million tons of charcoal is this way used each year. This over-consumption is not sustainable and is an important reason behind the acute deforestation and soil erosion problems found in this country. On top of that, emissions of greenhouse gas resulting from the burning of charcoal, significantly participate to the global problem that is climate change. To deal with this issue, the French NGO Entrepreneurs du Monde launched a new program called PALMIS Enèji with the objective to facilitate access to cleaner, more modern and cheaper sources of energy for all. This program works as a social micro-franchise that distribute more efficient charcoal cookstoves, LGP cookstoves and solar lanterns. PALMIS Enèji is developing its own distribution network with the objective of making those products easily available to all. A new microcredit financial product is also being developed with the support of ID Microfinance (a local microfinance institution and also a program of Entrepreneurs du Monde) to help people with limited financial means to have to access to those products. Finally, PALMIS Enèji is trying to increase the level of awareness in local populations about the described issues and the advantages of those products by creating communication tools tailored to the local context. The next step will very likely be the creation of a social enterprise in order to assure the sustainability of its social mission: to distribute as much as possible energy products in Haiti. The project activity “Expanding LPG access in Haiti through microfinance services" is in phase with this approach since it aims to promote the use of LPG as a source of energy for cooking, thus limiting the usage of charcoal and thus reducing emissions of greenhouse gas. Other than the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions and helping fighting deforestation, this project also offers the possibility to reduce the emissions of toxic gas such as carbon monoxide inside households. Indeed, the combustion of charcoal with traditional stoves, generates toxic gas in the air. Finally, the use of LGP cook stove, instead of a traditional one, means the end user is saving significant amount of money because less fuel is needed for her/his cooking needs.

Mahasakthi MAC Samakhya Ltd, a registered autonomous body, is an apex federation of four Mutually Aided Thrift Cooperative Societies of women promoted by the NGO - Timbaktu Collective. The four Cooperative societies; Adisakthi, Ananthasakthi, Mahilasakthi and Durgasakthi cooperatives are located in Chennekothapalli, Roddam, Ramagiri and Penukonda Mandals respectively in Anantapur district, Andhra Pradesh, India and are functional in the region for nearly one and a half decades. Mahasakthi Cooperative Federation encourages independent, sustainable and viable alternative economic institutions of women focussing on women’s leadership, their legal rights and political empowerment. The purpose of the project activity is to set up 6,000 biogas plants (digesters) of 2m3 capacity each for single households having minimum of two cows and place to build biogas digester in four Mandals of Anantapur district, Andhra Pradesh, and in this way replace Non-Renewable Biomass with biogas for cooking and heating water. A biogas plant of 2 m3 capacity is sufficient to provide cooking fuel to a family of four to five . Anantapur district in Andhra Pradesh State is a biomass deficit region . Fuel wood scarcity has an impact directly on rural households, which are highly dependent on this fuel. Demand for fuel wood and logs from commons and forests have caused resource degradation to the extent that collection exceeds sustainable yield. Forest degradation on the other hand leads to fuel wood scarcity leading to unsustainable removal of biomass to meet the demands. The project activity will attenuate the rural thermal energy needs used for cooking and water heating. Each household will install a 2 m3 biogas plant and cattle dung will be put into the anaerobic digester (Deenabandhu biogas Model). The technology is tried and tested in India , and has been in use for many years. By utilizing this cattle dung in a controlled anaerobic digestion and combustion system, biogas will be available for cooking energy and heating water. Biogas will be used on a two-ring gas stove having 4 inch burner, with a flame temperature of 870oC , supplied as part of the project activity. Implementation of the project depends on the successful validation and registration as a CDM project activity since the project will be financed completely from carbon revenues. After the project is registered as a CDM activity, carbon forward funding will enable the construction of domestic bio-digesters. An end user agreement will be signed between the PP, the Mahasakthi MAC Samakhya Ltd and the end user after construction, wherein the end user is aware of emission reductions from the use of biogas, and are willing to give up their rights and transfer the credit ownership to the Project Proponent, the Mahasakthi MAC Samakhya Ltd. Each household will feed cattle dung into the anaerobic digester which is a renewable source. The methane from the digester will be burnt to generate thermal energy thus replacing non-renewable firewood. By utilizing these various sources of biogenic waste in a controlled anaerobic digestion and combustion system, biogas will be available for cooking and heating water.

The purpose of the project activity is to use the wind energy potential in the North West coastal belt of Sri Lanka to produce a total of 10 MW using eight wind turbines, each rated at 1.25 MW. The power plant is expected to generate a net energy output of 27.638 GWh per year, estimated on the basis of long-term average wind speeds at the location. Electricity produced is sold to Ceylon Electricity Board (CEB), the national electricity utility, through a dedicated transmission line. The Project has been designated by the Sri Lanka Sustainable Energy Authority (SLSEA) and Ceylon Electricity Board (CEB) as a Small Power Project (SPP), and its operations and sale of electricity are governed by the Permit issued by SLSEA, and the standardised Small Power Purchase Agreement (SPPA) signed with CEB. The Permit was issued and the SPPA was executed, before the commencement of construction activities. The SPPA is a standardised, 20-year, non-negotiable contract, and defines a standardised tariff for the sale of electricity on the basis of a generic wind power plant and other financial indices at the time of calculating the tariff by the Authority (SLSEA). This project is the first wind power project in Sri Lanka. The energy generated by the project is to be supplied to the sole purchaser of electricity in the country, the Ceylon Electricity Board. The metering of the generation will take place at the panel room of the project, where all eight WTGs will be connected. The metering of the project is done by the CEB, and at the commissioning of the project, the officials from the CEB will connect the meters for the metering. The project activity reduces greenhouse gas emissions in the following manner. The wind resource potential is converted to electricity using eight wind turbines and electricity is supplied to the national grid, which is fully owned and managed by CEB. Sri Lanka’s electricity generating system feeding the national grid is dominated by thermal power plants, using diesel, fuel oil and naphtha, and is also using coal from year 2011. A range of diesel engines, open cycle gas turbines and combined cycle gas turbines serve the grid, while the first coal-fired power plant in Sri Lanka commenced operation in March 2011 at a site adjacent to this small scale CDM project activity. Energy share in the national grid from fossil-fuelled thermal power plants was 60% in 2007, and is expected to exceed 80% by year 2020. Electricity generated from the Mampuri Wind Power Plant displaces a corresponding portion of fossil fuels used in power plants serving the national grid and avoids the corresponding greenhouse gas emissions from the oil and coal power plants. The Mampuri Wind Power Plant is estimated to displace 18,768 tCO2 per year at an emission factor of 0.6791 kgCO2 per kWh, as calculated later in this PDD. It also avoids other emissions such as SOx and NOx from thermal power plants located throughout Sri Lanka. The project activity has improved the road along the coast at Mampuri, which has enhanced the mobility of villagers in Mampuri. Several community service initiatives are being implemented by the project participant. Estimated project start date: 23/08/2008

BaumInvest has implemented a pioneering reforestation project in northern Costa Rica that combines ecological sustainability with social responsibility. The project focuses on transforming degraded pasturelands, previously used for extensive cattle ranching, into thriving forests of tropical hardwoods using a proven, nature-based approach. These mixed stands primarily consist of native species alongside teak, promoting biodiversity and ecosystem resilience. Spanning four reforestation sites in remote northern Costa Rica, the project covers a total area of 1538 hectares, with 978 hectares certified under the Gold Standard for reforestation. Approximately 20% of the project area remains untouched as old-growth and secondary forest, as well as wetlands, which serve as crucial habitats and biological corridors for endangered species. One of the project’s areas, La Virgen is situated near Braulio Carrillo National Park further enhancing its ecological significance. Managing the reforested areas sustainably is a key priority of the project, which includes the practice of selective harvesting. By selectively harvesting individual trees rather than clear-cutting large areas, the project not only supports long-term forest health and biodiversity but also enhances carbon sequestration. Additionally, the project is situated within two UNESCO-recognized biosphere reserves, Agua y Paz and 'Cordillera Volcánica Central.

The project activity involves the construction of a hydropower plant with 02 units in Vinh Kim commune, Vinh Thanh district, Binh Dinh province of Vietnam. The main structure of hydropower plant includes a dam, intake, tunnel, pressurized well, penstock, power house and a discharge channel.Prior to the implementation of the project activity, electricity in Vietnam is generated mainly from fossil fuel sources and is solely distributed to consumers via the unique national electricity grid. The project’s purpose is to generate hydroelectricity by installation of water turbines and generators from a clean and renewable source to supply to the national grid via a Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) signed with the Electricity Corporation of Vietnam (EVN). The project's installed capacity and estimated annual gross power generation is 28 MW and 119,500 MWh , respectively. The net electricity generated (with an estimated annual volume of 118,305 MWh ) will be supplied to the national grid via a newly constructed 110kV transmission line which will connect between the plant and a transformer station.The baseline scenario of the project activity is the same as the scenario existing prior to the start of implementation of the project activity.The project activity will generate renewable power with negligible GHG emissions, which will displace part of the electricity otherwise supplied by fossil fuel fired power plants. As the power density of reservoir is above 10 W/m2, no GHG emissions from the reservoirs need to be accounted in the project activity. Thus, GHG emission reductions can be achieved via this proposed project activity.

The project activity is a poultry litter based power project in Thakkellapalli village, Yacharam mandal, Ranga Reddy District of Andhra Pradesh, India. The project has an installed capacity of 7.5 MW and utilizes poultry litter, which is a waste product of the local poultry farming industry and is presently dumped in pits near the poultry farms resulting in emissions of methane to the atmosphere. The project activity also utlilizes other biomass, such as rice husk. In the absence of the project activity the grid dominated thermal power plants would generate an equivalent quantity of power, resulting in GHG emissions as per the carbon intensity of the fuel mix constituting the grid, and the poultry litter would be continued to be dumped in the anaerobic lagoons in the fields, resulting in GHG emissions as per the carbon intensity of methane.
